subject: Re: Private GPU pool — multi-tenant QoS buckets and per-tenant admission budgets
messages:
From: Paul Singh <paul.singh@acmecloud.com>
To: Logan Wright <logan_wright@redwood.ai>
Cc: infra-ops@acmecloud.com
Date: Mon, 17 Aug 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Private GPU pool: capacity + per-tenant QoS ask

Hi Logan,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We're moving toward an initial carveout of a private GPU pool in our us-west VPC and need operational guidance for two things before procurement: 

1) How to set per-tenant admission budgets so one noisy tenant doesn't cause SLA regressions for others (our workloads are mixed: chat, embeddings, and long-form completions).
2) A simple capacity scheme (slots / QPS buckets) that we can use to size minimum reserved capacity and a burst buffer.

Can your team share an ops playbook or a short worksheet we can use to run numbers against our traffic mix? Ideally something that ties QoS buckets to throughput targets and visible metrics for alerting.

Paul
Infra Ops, Acme Cloud
(Attachment: initial-traffic-sample.csv)

From: Logan Wright <logan_wright@redwood.ai>

Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 17 Aug 2026 11:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Private GPU pool: capacity + per-tenant QoS ask

Paul — thanks, we can absolutely help. High level: we recommend combining fixed admission buckets (guaranteed QPS) + elastic burst credits (shared burst pool) + tenant-level shaping based on token‑per‑second cost profiles.

I've attached a concise ops playbook and a calculator that maps traffic mix to GPU slot equivalents and burst buffer sizing. Quick notes below; we'll follow up with a short runbook you can drop into your runbooks.

Key proposals (summary):
- Define three QoS tiers: critical (guaranteed), best-effort (elastic), and burst (shared short-term).
- Map tenant SLAs to guaranteed QPS buckets expressed in token/sec and converted to GPU slot units using model-specific throughput factors (e.g., small-chat model: 8k tokens/sec per T4 equivalency; long-form model: 1.5k tokens/sec).
- Reserve a base pool for guaranteed buckets (sum of guaranteed slot units). Size base pool = sum(guaranteed slots) + 20% safety margin for eviction/latency jitter.
- Maintain burst pool = 15-30% of base pool, with admission-credit tokens consumed per request and replenishment at controlled rate (to prevent sustained tail-churn).
- Enforce tenant shaping at the load balancer + request router layer to avoid cross-tenant KV-cache pollution; tag incoming requests with tenant_id and qos_tier.

Action items we need from Acme to run a tailored calc:
1) 7-day percentile traffic by tenant (p50/p95/p99) for request rate and average tokens per request.
2) Model mix (which models each tenant uses) and per-model perf profile (tokens/sec on target hardware).
3) Expected growth window and acceptable failover behavior (throttle vs degrade quality).

Deliverables: attached playbook (qos-buckets-proposal.pdf) and calc (tenant-admission-calc.xlsx). If you can share the traffic sample, Karthik and I will run the numbers and propose a staging/prod carveout size.

I'll loop Marissa for deployment ops checklist (networking / egress limits).

—Logan
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
(Attachment: qos-buckets-proposal.pdf)

Paul — gave the attachments a quick pass and ran a baseline using the sample traffic. A few technical clarifications and recommendations from the runtime side: 

1) Model throughput normalization: we convert everything to "GPU-slot-seconds" where 1 slot-second = throughput of 1 standard unit (example: A100-40GB @ our inference kernel for model X). This lets you mix model types. See tab "Normalization" in the calculator.

2) KV cache contamination: long-form persona workloads will warm large KV caches. We recommend tenant cache namespaces + per-tenant cache eviction priority to keep guaranteed-tier latencies bounded. Without namespace isolation, a single tenant can evict others' hot prefixes and cause p95 spikes.

3) Networking/egress headroom: plan for 30% overhead on inter-node traffic during peak batching windows (this is primarily due to KV sync + attention exchange for multiplexed inference). Ensure your VPC route tables and egress NAT instances have that headroom baked into provisioning.

4) Admission math (quick):
- Guaranteed pool = SUM(tenant_guaranteed_qps * avg_tokens_per_request / model_tokens_per_sec) rounded up to nearest slot. + 20% margin.
- Burst pool = max(ceil(0.2 * guaranteed_pool), min_burst_slots(4)).

5) Observability: emit tenant-level token/sec, slot-utilization, batch-latency histogram, and cache-eviction-rate. Create alerts: tenant_slot_utilization > 80% sustained for 5m, overall_slot_saturation > 90% for 2m.

I'll run a fuller variant for Acme if you share a 7-day export. Marissa, David — can you validate the networking checklist and procurement sizing assumptions?

-Karthik
Principal Runtime Engineer
Redwood Inference

Paul — looping in the deployment checklist and a conservative initial carveout proposal for staging/prod. I've run the sample through the spreadsheet and included two sizing options attached: conservative and performance-forward.

Staging (conservative):
- Base pool: 12 GPU-slot equivalents (covers guaranteed buckets at p95 with 20% margin).
- Burst pool: 3 slots (25% of base).
- Networking: allocate 40 Gbps egress NAT headroom and enable cross-subnet MTU to avoid fragmentation for large batch payloads.
- Policies: tenant cache namespaces enabled, per-tenant ingress policer to cap sustained QPS above guaranteed buckets.

Prod (performance-forward):
- Base pool: 20 GPU-slot equivalents (covers p99 bursts + 30% margin).
- Burst pool: 6 slots (30% of base).
- Networking: 80 Gbps egress headroom, dedicated NAT gateway pair for the carveout, and explicit route table for cross-AZ traffic.

Operational runbook highlights:
- Warmup: pre-warm KV caches for critical tenants during cutover window (use synthetic requests at low TTLs to populate prefixes).
- Failover: if overall_slot_saturation > 95% for 1m, automatically degrade best-effort tier and reroute new requests to hosted fallback variants (documented fallback endpoints in the playbook).
- Monitoring: run an hourly tenant headroom report. Weekly capacity review with infra to decide when to expand base/burst pools.

Next steps: Paul, if you can confirm which tenants are critical vs best-effort and share a 7-day export, we'll produce a final carveout recommendation and a deployment checklist you can hand to your infra team.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Product Operations Lead, Redwood Inference
